newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity called steady to lower with OTC.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity called steady to lower with OTC.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were called to open steady to lower Wednesday in line with over-the-counter (OTC) trading amid a short-term tightness in hydroelectric supply in the Pacific Northwest.
Market sources said forecasts of mild summer across of the West also put downward pressure on OTC prices.

In OTC activity, September Palo Verde (PV) futures were quoted at $29.00-29.50 a megawatt hour (MWh) down from Tuesday's settlement at $29.77 and September California-Oregon Border (COB) was talked $22.10-22.50 steady from yesterday's close at $22.48.
Day-ahead power prices at PV eased to $33.00-34.00 a MWh on projection of moderate air-conditioning demand, but those at COB firmed to $19.50-22.00 due to supply tightness, market sources said.
Slower discharge from the 6,150 MW Grand Coulee hydropower dam, the uppermost U.S. project on the Columbia River, will mean less power generation through Monday.
Less flow through Grand Coulee project stemmed from plans to refill reservoirs in U.S. and Canada.

Three western power units--a 260 MW Hayden coal-fired unit in Colorado, a 550 MW Jim Bridger coal-fired unit in Wyoming, and a 600 MW Grand Coulee hydroturbine in Washington--are set to resume operation today after unplanned repairs.
The 254 MW unit 1 at the Valmy coal-fired power plant in Nevada will likely be off line for a week after being shut Monday due to a rotor problem.
The 750 MW Four Corners coal-fired unit 5 in New Mexico, shut earlier this month to repair a high pressure generator field, was planned to restart next week.
The 1,221 MW Palo Verde 2 nuclear power unit in Arizona began slowly coasting down to its September refueling outage.

Capacity on the Pacific Intertie transmission system, the main conduit that moves cheap Northwest hydropower to southern California, should be raised by 600 megawatts (MW) to 6,900 MW no later than 2400 PDT on Monday.
The Intertie's current 6,300 MW rating will expire Thursday, but the limit would likely be extended if the new rating is not implemented by then.

The latest six to 10 day forecasts showed the West would experience seasonal to slightly cooler-than-seasonal readings regionwide with a monsoonal flow bringing above-normal precipitation in the mountainous areas.
